item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers' trade for infielder Royce Lewis and decision not to non-tender outfielder Alex Call were the stories of Friday's deadline.
Call has been a candidate to be off the Dodgers roster since the trade deadline. However, he's continued to remain with the club.
Another player was non-tendered before Friday's deadline, though.
The Dodgers non-tendered right-handed pitcher Jake Cousins, who was a candidate for arbitration before he was designated for assignment earlier this week when the Dodgers added four prospects to their 40-man roster. Now, Cousins is officially a free agent after being non-tendered.
Jake Cousins Dodgers Tenure
Cousins, 32, joined the Dodgers last offseason on a one-year deal that paid him $950,000. He spent most of the season recovering from Tommy John surgery he underwent in June 2025. In September, he played in some rehab games for the Triple-A Oklahoma City Comets.
Across six games, Cousins allowed five runs over 4.1 innings for a 10.38 ERA. He had five walks to four strikeouts and allowed four hits.
Jake Cousins MLB Career
Cousins was initially drafted by the Washington Nationals in the 20th round of the 2017 draft.
He was released ahead of the 2019 season and went to the independent Frontier League. Then, midway through the 2019 season, the Milwaukee Brewers purchased his contract.
Cousins made his MLB debut with the Brewers in 2021, finishing with a 2.70 ERA across 30 innings. He then again had a 2.70 ERA in 2022 across 13.1 innings, but dealt with an elbow injury for much of the year.
Since 2023, Cousins has bounced around with the Brewers, Houston Astros, Chicago White Sox and New York Yankees organizations. In 2024, he made 37 appearances for the Yankees, finishing with a 2.37 ERA and 53 strikeouts over 38 innings.
The right-hander opened the 2025 season on the injured list with an elbow injury. He ended up undergoing Tommy John surgery, and has been working his way back ever since.
Cousins should be ready for the start of the 2027 season, and thus could have a market for a major league deal this offseason. If not, he could sign a minor league deal with an invitation to spring training, and then look to work his way onto a team's Opening Day roster.
Who Did the Dodgers Tender a Contract To?
In addition to avoiding arbitration with Call, the Dodgers tendered contracts to four players: outfielder Andy Pages and right-handed pitchers Brock Stewart, Emmet Sheehan and Gavin Stone.
The team also traded for infielder Royce Lewis from the Minnesota Twins in exchange for right-handed pitcher Bobby Miller and catching prospect Francisco Espinoza.

item.content:encoded:
It's been a newsy week in baseball, between owners meetings, Tarik Skubal's free agency, and the deadline to protect prospects from the Rule 5 Draft.
The Dodgers had a meeting scheduled with Skubal, put four prospects on the 40-man roster and announced that reliever Seth Halverson had undergone Tommy John surgery.
With all that action, and end of the current CBA fast approaching on Dec. 1, it's a good time to evaluate the Dodgers' pitching staff:
Starting rotation
Returning: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski, Emmet Sheehan
Free agent: Tarik Skubal, Eric Lauer
Additional depth: Gavin Stone
Skubal essentially replaced Ohtani, limited by injuries to his left knee and right biceps, in the rotation when the Dodgers acquired the left-hander at the trade deadline. But if they don't re-sign Skubal, it won't be as simple as Ohtani tagging back in. The Dodgers still have to work out his workload for next year, as he returns to two-way duties.
The Dodgers do have pitching depth, with a promising trio of Sasaki, Wrobleski and Sheehan rounding out the back of the rotation, and Stone expected to be healthy next year, but the Dodgers' commitment to a six-man rotation requires a wealth of options. They also aren't looking to coast after an NLCS exit. And raising the bar from 2026 could mean supplementing the rotation, whether that be with Skubal or another starter via free agency or trade.
"Do you need it? I don't know. Do you want it? Maybe," general manager Brandon Gomes said at the MLB general manager meetings last week. "You may not know that you need it until it's too late. … The floor right now is really high. We do have a good amount of depth in our pitching, so now it's just taking into account what makes sense for us based on different avenues of how things shake out."
Bullpen
Returning (min 10 IP in 2026 season): Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Edgardo Henriquez, Jack Dreyer, Will Klein, Brock Stewart, Kyle Hurt, Landon Knack
Out: Evan Phillips (signed with Braves), Seth Halvorsen (Tommy John surgery)
Free agent: Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen, Brusdar Graterol, Kris Bubic
Phillips' three-year, $35 million deal helped set the early bullpen market. He returns to the Braves, the team that drafted him in 2015, after six years with the Dodgers.
It was always clear that the Dodgers would have work to do this offseason reinforcing their bullpen, a common winter project for most teams around the league. Though the Dodgers have signed closers (Scott and Díaz) in back-to-back offseasons, both of whom remain under contract, manager Dave Roberts regularly leaned on Phillips and Vesia in high-leverage situations.
Treinen hurt his shoulder during the last series of the regular season, and Graterol hasn't thrown in a major-league game since the 2024 World Series due to injuries. Bubic has traditionally been a starter, but after the Dodgers acquired him at the trade deadline, while he was still on the injured list, he worked back as a reliever to shorten his return timeline.
Halvorsen, the hard-throwing right-hander who the Dodgers acquired from the Rockies in late July, only made 11 major-league appearances with the Dodgers, but the 26-year-old showed plenty of potential. After undergoing Tommy John surgery on Tuesday he's expected to miss the 2027 season.
The reliever market started moving early, in an offseason that's expected to go into an indefinite hold when MLB owners impose a lockout, likely on Dec. 1.
40-man roster additions
In the face of a looming lockout this year, it's unclear whether there will actually be a Rule 5 Draft, which is typically held during the Winter Meetings in December. The last MLB lockout — which lasted 99 days, from December 2, 2021 to March 10, 2022 — completely wiped out the Rule 5 Draft.
Still, teams had to prepare this week as if it would happen. On Tuesday, the Dodgers added right-hander Christian Zazueta and left-handers Jackson Ferris, Adam Serwinowski and Luke Fox to the 40-man roster. To make room for them, the Dodgers designated right-handed pitcher Jake Cousins and infielder Christian Cairo for assignment.
Zazueta (No.5), Serwinowski (No. 14) and Ferris (No. 17), are all ranked by MLB Pipeline among the top 20 prospects in the Dodgers' system, and Zazueta is ranked No. 33 in MLB.
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Why Re-Signing Evan Phillips is a Must For the Dodgers This Offseason
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers saw eight players enter free agency this offseason, and Evan Phillips is one of a few players who could still have a big role for the Dodgers next year. Phillips isn’t the most important player for the team to retain, as Tarik Skubal and Alex Vesia were both incredibly important to the team last year, but he played a key role in the bullpen during 2026. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers saw eight players enter free agency this offseason, and Evan Phillips is one of a few players who could still have a big role for the Dodgers next year.
Phillips isn’t the most important player for the team to retain, as Tarik Skubal and Alex Vesia were both incredibly important to the team last year, but he played a key role in the bullpen during 2026.
Why Should the Dodgers Keep Evan Phillips?
Phillips struggled upon his return for the Dodgers following Tommy John surgery, posting a 6.14 ERA through his eight games in July—his first month back.
After that, though, he had a couple of really impressive months to close the regular season. He posted a 2.61 ERA in August through 14 appearances, and had a 2.16 ERA through nine appearances in September.
On the year, Phillips had a 3.46 ERA through 26 innings, striking out 33 batters.
His fastball looked good throughout the season, averaging a career-best 96.8 mph during the season. His other pitches played well too, as is evident by his 31.1% strikeout rate and 35.4% chase rate.
Despite his strong chase numbers, though, Phillips was prone to giving up hard-hit fly balls and line drives, grading poorly with an average exit velocity of 91 mph and just a 31.8% ground ball rate. He allowed five home runs on the year, and definitely has to improve in that area if he’s to cut it for the Dodgers.
That being said, the Dodgers also lost Blake Treinen to free agency after the close of the season, and losing another right-handed veteran like Phillips would be a huge blow to their bullpen.
Phillips has historically performed well for the Dodgers over his six years with the team, posting a 2.36 ERA over the course of 232 games with Los Angeles. He is acclimated to high-leverage situations, having served as the Dodgers’ closer in 2023 and 2024, and would be a huge asset for the team.
Do the Dodgers Need Another Right-Handed Reliever?
As it stands, the Dodgers have several right-handers in their ranks, with Edwin Diaz, Edgardo Henriquez and Brock Stewart all commanding spots on the roster as well as Will Klein, Ben Casparius and Jake Cousins all recovering from injuries.
Even with their abundance of left-handers, the Dodgers would do well to keep Phillips as a middle-inning relief pitcher while Diaz, Henriquez and Tanner Scott handle late-inning duties.
While Phillips certainly wasn’t at his best last season, his track record and encouraging performances towards the end of the season warrant a spot on the team, especially for the price he commands.
Would you want the Dodgers to re-sign Evan Phillips?
